(أَنَا شَهِيدٌ عَلَى هَؤُلَاءِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ) [I am a witness over these on the Day of Resurrection]. He said: This indicates that they are specially distinguished, and that no one else shares this with them. Abu 'Umar said: This resembles an anomalous view (shudhudh), and the position that their ritual washing (ghusl) should be abandoned is more correct, because this is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the martyrs of Uhud and others. Abu Dawud related from Jabir, who said: A man was struck by an arrow in his chest or throat and died, so he was wrapped in his garments as he was. He said: And we were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second issue: as for the funeral prayer (salat) over them, the scholars differed on this as well. Malik, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Dawud held that no funeral prayer is to be offered over them, based on the hadith of Jabir, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to bring together two men from the martyrs of Uhud in a single garment, then he would say: "Which of them had more memorization of the Qur'an?" When one of them was pointed out to him, he would place him first in the grave and say: "I am a witness over these on the Day of Resurrection." He ordered that they be buried in their blood, and they were not washed, and no funeral prayer was offered over them. The jurists of Kufa, Basra and Syria said: a funeral prayer is offered over them. They related many reports, most of which are mursal (reports in which the link to a Companion is missing), that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed over Hamzah and over all the martyrs of Uhud.

The fourth issue: The scholars agreed that a martyr who is carried away alive, does not die on the battlefield, lives and eats, then a funeral prayer is offered over him, just as was done for 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). They differed concerning one who was killed unjustly, such as those killed by the Kharijites, highway robbers and the like. Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said: Everyone who is killed unjustly is not washed, but a funeral prayer is offered over him and over every martyr; this is the view of all the people of Iraq. They related through many sound chains from Zayd ibn Suhan, who was killed on the day of the Camel: "Do not strip my garment from me, and do not wash the blood from me." It is established (thabata) from 'Ammar ibn Yasir that he said the same as Zayd ibn Suhan. 'Ammar ibn Yasir was killed at Siffin, and 'Ali did not wash him. Al-Shafi'i had two opinions: one of them is that he is washed like all the dead, except one killed by the enemy in war, and this is the view of Malik. Malik said: One killed by the disbelievers and who dies on the battlefield is not washed. But one who was killed other than on the battlefield, killed by disbelievers, is washed and a funeral prayer is offered over him. This is the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah be pleased with him). The other opinion of al-Shafi'i is: the one killed among the rebels (baghi) is not washed. The view of Malik is more sound, for the washing of the dead is established by consensus (ijma') and by the transmission of the whole community. Therefore the washing of every deceased person is obligatory, except one whom a consensus or an established Sunnah has excluded. And success is from Allah.

The fifth issue: If the enemy attacks a people in their dwelling and they do not know of it, and kills some of them, is his ruling that of one killed on the battlefield, or the ruling of all other dead? This question arose for us in Cordoba, may Allah restore it: the enemy raided, may Allah defeat him, at dawn on the third of the honoured Ramadan, in the year 627 AH, while the people were in their courtyards, heedless. He killed and took captives, and among those killed was my father, may Allah have mercy on him. I asked our shaykh, the reciter and teacher Abu Ja'far Ahmad, known as Abu Hijjah [in (j): "Ibn Hijjah"], and he said: Wash him and pray over him, for your father was not killed on the battlefield between the two lines. Then I asked our shaykh Rabi' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad ibn Rabi' ibn Ubayy, and he said: His ruling is the ruling of those killed on the battlefield. Then I asked the chief judge of the community Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Qatral, while around him was a group of jurists, and they said: Wash him, shroud him and pray over him, so I did that. Afterwards I came across the question in "al-Tabsirah" of Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi and others. Had that been before, I would not have washed him, but would have buried him in his blood in his garments.

The sixth issue: This verse indicates the great reward of being killed in the way of Allah, and of martyrdom in it, to the extent that it expiates sins, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Being killed in the way of Allah expiates everything except debt; so Jibril (peace be upon him) told me just now." Our scholars said: The mention of debt is an alert to what has the same meaning among the rights bound up with obligations (dhimam), such as usurpation (ghasb), taking property unjustly, intentional killing and wounding, and other liabilities. For all of this is more deserving not to be forgiven by jihad than debt, since it is more severe. Retribution in all of this is by good deeds and bad deeds, as the established Sunnah has related. 'Abd Allah ibn Unays related, saying: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah will gather the servants, or he said the people (Hammam, a narrator in this chain, was uncertain), and he pointed with his hand toward Syria, naked, uncircumcised (ghurul), empty-handed (buhm)." We said: "What is buhm?" He said: "They have nothing with them. Then He will call them with a voice that will be heard by those who are near and those who are far: 'I am the King, I am the Judge. No one among the people of Paradise should enter Paradise while one of the people of the Fire seeks him for an injustice, and no one among the people of the Fire should enter the Fire while one of the people of Paradise seeks him for an injustice, even a slap.'" He said: We said: "How, when we come to Allah barefoot, naked and uncircumcised?" He said: "By good deeds and bad deeds." (Related by al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah [in (j): "Umamah"; the correct reading is what is given here, as in al-Tamhid].)

In Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you know who is bankrupt (muflis)?" They said: "The bankrupt among us is one who has no dirham and no goods." He said: "The bankrupt of my community is one who comes on the Day of Resurrection with prayer, fasting and zakat, and comes having reviled this one, slandered that one, consumed the property of this one, shed the blood of this one and beaten this one. So this one is given from his good deeds, and that one from his good deeds. If his good deeds are exhausted before he has settled what is upon him, then some of their sins are taken and cast upon him, then he is thrown into the Fire." The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if a man were killed in the way of Allah, then brought to life, then killed, then brought to life, then killed, while he had a debt upon him, he would not enter Paradise until it is settled on his behalf." Abu Hurayrah related: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The soul of the believer is suspended as long as he has a debt." Ahmad ibn Zuhayr said: Yahya ibn Ma'in was asked about this hadith and said: "It is sound."

If it is said: This indicates that some of the martyrs do not enter Paradise from the moment of death, and their spirits are not in the crops of birds as I mentioned to you, and they are not in their graves; so where are they? We say: It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The spirits of the martyrs are at a river at the gate of Paradise called Barik; their provision comes out to them from Paradise morning and evening." Perhaps these are the ones. And Allah knows best. For this reason Imam Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyyah said: "These are categories and differing conditions, unified by the fact that they are 'provided for' (yurzaqun)."

Imam Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Yazid ibn Majah al-Qazwini has related in his Sunan, from Sulaym ibn 'Amir, who said: I heard Abu Umamah say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The martyr of the sea is like two martyrs of the land, and the one who is tossed upon the sea is like one who writhes in his blood on land, and what is between the two waves is like one who cuts the world in obedience to Allah. Allah, mighty and majestic, has entrusted the Angel of Death with taking souls, except the martyrs of the sea, for He, glory be to Him, Himself takes their souls, and He forgives the martyr of the land all his sins except debt, and He forgives the martyr of the sea all his sins, including debt." [In the commentary on al-Jami', it is with the dual form (shahidayy).] (Al-ma'id: one whose head spins from the wind of the sea and the tossing of the ship with the waves. Tashahhut: one who writhes and thrashes about in his blood.)

The seventh issue: The debt which holds its owner back from Paradise, and Allah knows best, is that which he left no means of repayment for and did not bequeath, or he was able to pay but did not pay, or he incurred it through extravagance or foolishness and died without settling it. As for one who incurred debt for an obligatory right out of poverty and hardship, and died without leaving means of repayment, Allah will not hold him back from Paradise, if Allah wills, because it is an obligation on the ruler to pay his debt on his behalf, either from the general sadaqat, or from the share of the debtors (al-gharimin), or from the fay' that returns to the Muslims. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever leaves a debt or dependants (diya'an) [al-diya': (with an initial fatha) dependants], then it is upon Allah and His Messenger; and whoever leaves property, it is for his heirs." We have elaborated this subject further in the book "al-Tadhkirah", and praise be to Allah.

The second point: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ يُرْزَقُونَ﴾ [they are provided for with their Lord]. Here there is an elision of a qualifier, its implied meaning being: "with the honour of their Lord." And "'inda" here implies the utmost nearness, so it is like "ladā" (at, with), and therefore it is not diminutive, so one does not say "'unayd," as Sibawayh said. This is the nearness of honour, not the nearness of distance and proximity. And "yurzaqun" is the familiar provision of ordinary usage. Whoever says: It is the life of remembrance, says: they are provided with fine praise. The first is the literal meaning. It has been said: The spirits perceive, in that state in which they wander, the fragrances of Paradise, its goodness, its delights and its joy, what befits spirits, by which they are nourished and revived. As for bodily pleasures, when those spirits are returned to their bodies they will fully enjoy all the bliss that Allah has prepared for them. This is a fine view, though it contains some kind of metaphor, and it accords with what we have chosen. And the granter of success is God. [The word] (فرحين) [rejoicing] is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yurzaqun." In ordinary speech "farihun" is permitted as a description of the living. It derives from "al-farah," meaning joy. The bounty (al-fadl) in this verse is the bliss mentioned. Ibn al-Sumayqa read "farihin" with an alif, and both are dialectal forms, like "al-farih" and "al-farih," "al-hadhir" and "al-hadhir," "al-tami'" and "al-tami'," "al-bakhil" and "al-bakhil." Al-Nahhas said: Outside the Qur'an it is permitted to read it in the nominative, as a description of the living.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿وَيَسْتَبْشِرُونَ بِالَّذِينَ لَمْ يَلْحَقُوا بِهِمْ مِنْ خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ [and they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them]. The meaning is: they have not yet joined them in excellence, though they too have excellence. Its root is from "al-bashrah" (skin of the face), because when a person rejoices the effect of happiness appears on his face. Al-Suddi said: The martyr is brought a book in which is mention of those of his brothers who will come after him, so he rejoices as the people of an absent one rejoice at his arrival in the world. Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, al-Rabi' and others said: Their rejoicing is that they say: "Our brothers whom we left behind us in the world are fighting in the way of Allah with their Prophet, and they will be martyred and attain the same honour as we are in; so they are delighted and rejoice for them in that." It has also been said: The reference of the rejoicing to "those who have not yet joined them" is to all the believers, even if they were not killed. But when they witnessed the reward of Allah, certainty settled that the religion of Islam is the truth by which Allah rewards, so they rejoice for themselves at what Allah has given them of His bounty, and rejoice for the believers that no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Furak held this meaning.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 3, verse 171:

﴿They rejoice in favour from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not allow to be lost the reward of the believers﴾ (3:171). That is, [they rejoice] in a garden (jannah) from Allah. It is also said: in forgiveness from Allah.

(Wa-fadl) [bounty] here is for added clarification. Bounty (fadl) is included within favour (ni'mah), and this indicates its vastness and that it is not like the favours of this world. It has also been said: bounty came after favour for emphasis. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The martyr has six qualities with Allah" (so it is in al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, "six," and in counting it is seven [[In the margin of al-Sindi's commentary on Sunan Ibn Majah: "His saying 'six qualities' as mentioned is seven, unless the granting of protection and security from terror is counted as one."]]): "He is forgiven at the first gush [[Dafa'ah: al-Damiri said: we have it vocalized in Jami' al-Tirmidhi with a damma on the dal, and so the lexicographers said: al-dufa'ah (with damma) is what is poured out of a vessel or waterskin at once, and likewise the dufa'ah of rain and the like, similar to the dufqah with a qaf. As for al-daf'ah (with fatha), it is a single time, so it does not fit here.]] of his blood; he sees his place in Paradise; he is protected from the punishment of the grave; he is secure from the greatest terror; a crown of dignity is placed on his head, a ruby of which is better than the world and what is in it; he is married to seventy-two wives from the wide-eyed houris; and he intercedes for seventy of his relatives."

He said: This is a hadith that is hasan sahih gharib. This is an explanation of favour and bounty. The reports on this meaning are numerous. It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: "Swords are the keys to Paradise." It is also narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah the Exalted has honoured the martyrs with five honours with which He has not honoured any of the prophets, nor myself, being one of them: first, that the angel of death took the souls of all the prophets, and he is the one who will take my soul, whereas as for the martyrs, Allah Himself takes their souls by His power however He wills, and He does not give the angel of death authority over their souls; second, that all the prophets were washed after death, and I too will be washed after death, whereas the martyrs are not washed and have no need of the water of this world; third, that all the prophets were shrouded, and I too will be shrouded, whereas the martyrs are not shrouded but are buried in their garments; fourth, that when the prophets died they were called dead, and when I die it will be said that he has died, whereas the martyrs are not called dead; fifth, that the prophets are given intercession on the Day of Resurrection, and my intercession too is on the Day of Resurrection, whereas the martyrs intercede every day for whomever they wish."

His saying, [may He be exalted]: (And that Allah) [Ibn Kathir?] — al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the alif (wa-inna), and the rest read it with a fatha (wa-anna). Whoever reads with a fatha, its meaning is: they rejoice in a favour from Allah, and they rejoice that Allah does not allow to be lost the reward of the believers. Whoever reads with a kasra, it is on the basis of a new sentence (ibtida'). Its evidence is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And Allah does not allow to be lost the reward of the believers."

"Alladhina" (الَّذِينَ) is in the nominative case, as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "min ba'di ma asabahumu al-qarh" (مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا أَصابَهُمُ الْقَرْحُ). It may also be in the genitive case, as a substitute (badal) [[As in the original manuscripts. The text of al-Nahhas, from which this is quoted, reads: badalan.]] of "al-mu'minin" or of "bi-alladhina lam yalhaqu" (بِالَّذِينَ لَمْ يَلْحَقُوا).

"Istajabu" (اسْتَجابُوا) means "ajabu" (أَجَابُوا), and the sin and ta' are additional letters. From this is the line of poetry:

"So none answered him then, none responded" (فَلَمْ يَسْتَجِبْهُ عِنْدَ ذَاكَ مُجِيبُ) [[This is the second half of a line by Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi, lamenting his brother Abu al-Mighwar. Its first half is:

"And a caller who called, 'O one who answers the call to generosity!'"]]

In the two Sahihs, on the authority of 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said to me: "Your father was among those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had befallen them." This is the wording of Muslim. And from her, 'A'ishah said: "O son of my sister, your two fathers, meaning al-Zubayr and Abu Bakr, were among those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had befallen them." She also said: "When the polytheists withdrew from Uhud and the Prophet ﷺ and his companions were struck by what had struck them, he feared that they might return, so he said: 'Who will go out after these people until they know that we have strength?' So Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr went out with seventy men, and they set out on the trail of the people. They heard of them and returned with a blessing from Allah and grace."

'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) also referred to what happened in the expedition of Hamra' al-Asad, which lies about eight miles from Medina. That was on the day of Sunday, the second day after Uhud, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out to the people to pursue the polytheists, saying: "None goes out with us except those who fought there yesterday." So two hundred men of the believers rose up with him. In al-Bukhari it says: he said, "Who will go after them?" So seventy men from among them volunteered. He said: Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr were among them, as mentioned before, until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, instilling fear in the enemy. Some of them were heavily weighed down with wounds, unable to walk and finding no mount, so they were sometimes carried on the shoulders. All of that was in obedience to the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and out of eagerness for jihad.

It was also said that the verse was revealed concerning two men from Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal who were severely wounded, one of them leaning on his companion, and they went out with the Prophet ﷺ. When they reached Hamra' al-Asad, Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud met them and informed them that Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and those with him from Quraysh had gathered their forces and resolved to come back [[In other manuscripts: yarji'u (return).]] to Medina to annihilate its people. They said what Allah reported of them: "Hasbuna Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil" (Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs).

While Quraysh had resolved upon this, Ma'bad al-Khuza'i came to them. Khuza'ah were allies of the Prophet ﷺ and the confidants of his counsel. He had seen the condition of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and what they were upon. When he saw Quraysh's determination to return to annihilate the people of Medina, concern for that moved him, and he sincerely advised the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, so he warned Quraysh by saying to them: "I have left Muhammad and his Companions at Hamra' al-Asad with a great army, to which has gathered whoever had stayed behind from him, and they are burning with anger against you. So hurry, hurry! I forbid you from this. By Allah, what I saw has moved me to compose some verses of poetry about it." They said: "And what did you say?" He said: "I said:

"My mount was nearly broken by the noise, when the earth flowed with the swift, scattered horses [[Al-jurd: short-haired horses with thin skin. Ababil: troops.]]

They trample with noble lions, not stunted cowards [[Radat al-khayl radyan wa rudyanan: they struck the ground with their hooves in their going and running. Al-tanabilah: the short ones, singular tunbal. Al-umayl: one who leans upon the saddle and does not sit firmly on it. It was also said: he is the one who is lazy and does not ride or fight well. Al-ma'azil: people who have no weapons, singular ma'zal.]] at the meeting, nor are they limp-riders.

So I went on, thinking the earth was tilting, when they came with a leader not forsaken.

So I said: 'Woe to the son of Harb from your meeting, when Batha' boils with horses.' [[In al-Rawd al-Unuf: "taghatmatat al-Batha'" is a term borrowed from ghaghamah, the sound of a boiling pot. His words "al-khayl" (the horses); in Ha and Ibn Hisham, Turkey edition: al-jil. The first has a fault of prosody (sinad). Perhaps it is: al-khayl, plural of akhyal, which has no fault.]]

Indeed, I am a warner to the people of al-Basl, a warning of the morning, for everyone among them who is sharp of mind and understanding.

From the army of Ahmad, whose base-born [[Al-wakhsh: the lowly of people. Al-qanabil: a band of people or horses. In J, Z, and the Sirah of the Cairo edition with al-Rawd: tanabilah. In T, Y and H: tanatilah, from tanatala al-rajul, when a man becomes disgusted after cleanliness.]] troops are no match, and what I warned of cannot be described by hearsay.'"

He said: So that turned Abu Sufyan and those with him back, Allah cast terror into their hearts, and they returned to Mecca in fear, hastening. The Prophet ﷺ returned with his Companions to Medina, victorious, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So they returned with a blessing from Allah and grace, untouched by any harm﴾ [Al 'Imran: 174], meaning fighting and terror.

Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to go out with him, and he gave him permission. Allah the Exalted informed them that a great reward had been secured for them by this return. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It was an expedition (ghazwah)."

This is the interpretation of the majority concerning this verse. But Mujahid and 'Ikrimah (may Allah have mercy on them both) deviated and said: this verse, from His words "Those to whom the people said" up to His words "great" [Al 'Imran: 173-174], was revealed only concerning the Prophet's ﷺ going out to Badr al-Sughra. That was because he went out for the appointment of Abu Sufyan at Uhud, when he had said: "Our appointment is Badr, next year." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Say yes." So the Prophet ﷺ went out toward Badr, and there was a great market there. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave his Companions dirhams, and when he approached Badr, Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ash'ari came to him and informed him that Quraysh had gathered and were approaching to fight him, they and whoever joined them. The Muslims were apprehensive about this, but they said: "Hasbuna Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil," and they pressed on until they came to Badr, but found no one there. They found the market and bought with their dirhams food and merchandise, and they returned without meeting any harm, and they profited in their trade. Therefore, Allah's saying "So they returned with a blessing from Allah and grace" means: and grace in those trades. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 3, verse 173:

There is a difference of opinion regarding His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾. Mujahid, Muqatil, Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said: it refers to Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i. The wording is general but its meaning is specific, like His saying: ﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾ [al-Nisa': 54] [[See vol. 5, p. 250.]], meaning Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Suddi said: it refers to a Bedouin who was paid a fee for this. Ibn Ishaq and a group said: it means the people of the caravan of 'Abd al-Qays, who passed by Abu Sufyan, and he sent them to the Muslims to dissuade them. It was also said: "the people" here means the hypocrites. Al-Suddi said: When the Prophet ﷺ and his companions prepared to march to Badr al-Sughra for the appointment with Abu Sufyan, the hypocrites came to them and said: "We are your companions whom we forbade from going out to them, but you disobeyed us. They have fought you in your homes and prevailed. If you go to them in their homes, not one of you will return." They said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Abu Ma'shar said: some men from Hudhayl of the people of Tihamah entered Madinah, and the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked them about Abu Sufyan. They said: "They have gathered great hosts against you," "so fear them", i.e., be afraid of them and beware of them, for you have no power against them. Thus, according to these opinions, "the people" retains its general sense. And Allah knows best.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So it increased them in faith﴾, i.e., the saying of the people increased them in faith, meaning in assurance and certainty regarding their religion, and in steadfastness in their support, and in strength, boldness and readiness. Increase in faith according to this is in deeds. The scholars differed regarding the increase and decrease of faith in several opinions. The creed on this is that faith itself, which is one crown and one assurance in something, is merely a single essence, which does not admit an increase when it is present, nor does anything of it remain when it is removed. Thus there remains only that the increase and decrease occur in its objects, not in its essence. A group of scholars held that it increases and decreases with respect to the deeds that proceed from it, especially since many scholars apply the name "faith" to acts of obedience, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Faith has seventy-some branches, the highest of which is the statement 'There is no god but Allah,' and the lowest of which is removing harm from the road." Related by al-Tirmidhi, and Muslim added: "and modesty is a branch of faith." In the hadith of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Faith appears as a white spot in the heart; whenever faith increases, the spot increases." Regarding his words "lumazah" (white spot), al-Asma'i said: the lumazah is like a speck or similar whiteness, and from this it is said: "a horse with a lumazah," when there is some whiteness on its lips. The muhaddithun say "lamazah" with a fatha, but in Arabic speech it is with a damma, like shubhah, duhmah and khumrah. In it is proof against those who deny that faith increases and decreases. Do you not see that he says: whenever faith increases, the spot increases, until the whole heart becomes white. Likewise hypocrisy appears as a black spot in the heart; whenever hypocrisy increases, the heart blackens, until the whole heart becomes black. Some said: faith is an accident (ʿaraḍ), which does not persist for two moments, so it is renewed for the Prophet ﷺ and the righteous in succession; it increases by the succession of its like upon the heart of the believer, and by the continuity of its presence. It decreases by the succession of heedlessnesses upon the heart of the believer. Abu al-Ma'ali pointed to this. This meaning is found in the hadith of intercession, the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, related by Muslim. In it: "The believers will say: O our Lord, our brothers used to fast, pray and perform Hajj. He will say to them: Bring out those you recognize, and their forms will be forbidden to the Fire. They will bring out a great multitude whom the Fire has seized up to half their shins and to their knees. Then they will say: Our Lord, none remains in it of those You commanded us about. He will say: Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of a dinar of good, bring him out. They will bring out a great multitude. Then they will say: Our Lord, we have not left in it anyone of those You commanded us about. He will say: Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of half a dinar of good, bring him out. They will bring out a great multitude. Then they will say: Our Lord, we have not left in it anyone of those You commanded us about. He will say: Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of an atom of good, bring him out." And he mentioned the hadith [[Its remainder: "They will bring out a great multitude. Then they will say: Our Lord, we have not left in it any good." Muslim, vol. 1, p. 116.]]. It has been said that what is meant by faith in this hadith is the deeds of the heart, such as intention, sincerity, fear, sincere advice and the like. It was called faith because it is in the locus of faith, or faith is meant by way of the Arab custom of naming a thing by the name of what is adjacent to it or connected with it through a cause. The evidence for this interpretation is the saying of the intercessors, after bringing out those who had in their hearts the weight of an atom of good: "We have not left in it any good," although He, the Exalted, afterwards brings out many multitudes of those who say "There is no god but Allah," and they are certainly believers; had they not been believers, He would not have brought them out. Moreover, the first non-existence upon which the like is composed (in z: "yatarakkab") did not involve increase or decrease. This is estimated in motion. For when Allah, glory be to Him, creates a single knowledge and creates with it a like or likes of it with objects of knowledge, then His knowledge has increased; if Allah annihilates the likes, then it has decreased, i.e., the increase has ceased. Likewise when He creates a motion and creates with it a like or likes of it. A group of scholars held that the increase and decrease of faith is only by way of the proofs, so the proofs increase for one person, and it is said regarding that: it is an increase in faith; and in this sense, according to one of the opinions, the prophets were preferred over creation, for they knew it from many aspects, more than the aspects by which creation knows it. This view lies outside the implication of the verse, since it cannot be conceived that the increase in it is from the side of proofs. Another group held that the increase in faith is only by the descent of obligations and reports during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ, and in knowing them after ignorance over the long duration of time.

This is only an increase of faith, so the statement that faith increases is a metaphorical statement, and decrease cannot be conceived in it on this basis; it can only be conceived in relation to one who knows. So understand.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾, i.e., Allah is sufficient for us. "Hasb" is derived from "ihsab," which means sufficiency. The poet said:

"And she fills our house with aqit [[Aqit: something made from churned milk, left until it becomes solid.]] and ghee... and sufficient for your wealth is satiety and quenching."

Al-Bukhari related from Ibn Abbas, who said regarding His saying, the Exalted: "Those to whom the people said: Indeed the people have gathered against you—to His saying—"And they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Ibrahim the Friend, upon him be peace, said it when he was thrown into the Fire, and Muhammad ﷺ said it when the people said to them: Indeed the people have gathered against you. And Allah knows best.

Our scholars said: When they entrusted their affairs to Him and relied in their hearts upon Him, He gave them four kinds of reward: blessing (al-ni'mah), bounty (al-fadl), the averting of harm (sarf al-su'), and the following of His good pleasure (ittiba' al-rida). So they were pleased with Him, and He was pleased with them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 3, verse 175:

Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: The meaning is "it frightens you of its allies" (yukhawwifukum awliyahu), that is, "with its allies" (bi-awliyihi) or "from its allies" (min awliyihi). The preposition was dropped, the verb reached the noun directly, and it took the accusative. Like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿to warn of a severe punishment﴾ [al-Kahf: 2] [[See vol. 10, p. 246.]], meaning "to warn you of a severe punishment," that is, it frightens the believer with the disbeliever. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: The meaning is that it frightens its allies, the hypocrites, so that they would hold back from fighting the polytheists. As for the allies of Allah, they do not fear Him when He frightens them. It has also been said that what is meant is that this one who frightens you by gathering the disbelievers is a devil from among the devils of mankind, either Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud or someone else, according to the difference of opinion on that, as has already been mentioned.

(So do not fear them) means: do not fear the disbelievers mentioned in His saying, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you." Or it refers back to the allies, if you say that the meaning is "it frightens with its allies," that is, it frightens you with its allies.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and fear Me﴾ means: fear Me in abandoning My command, if you are believers in My promise. In the speech of the Arabs, khawf (fear) means dhuʿr (terror). Fulan frightened me (khawwafani fulan) and I feared him, meaning I was more fearful of him. Al-khawfaʾ (the desert) is a wasteland with no water in it. It is said: a she-camel khawfaʾ, which means mangy. Al-khafah is like al-kharitah (a pouch) made of leather, in which honey is extracted. Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah said: Some of the truthful ones (al-siddiqin) gathered before Ibrahim al-Khalil and said: "What is fear?" He said: "You are not secure until you reach the place of security." Sahl said: When al-Rabiʿ ibn Khaythum passed by a forge (kir), he would faint. This was mentioned to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, and he said: "When that happens to him, inform me." It happened to him, and they informed him. He came and put his hand into his shirt and found his heartbeat high, and he said: "I bear witness that this is the most fearful of the people of your time."

The one who fears Allah, the Exalted, is the one who fears that He will punish him, either in this world or in the Hereafter. For this reason it has been said: The one who fears is not the one who weeps and wipes his eyes, but the one who abandons what he fears he will be punished for. Allah, the Exalted, made fear of Him an obligation upon the servants, so He said: ﴿And fear Me, if you are believers﴾, and He said: ﴿And fear Me alone﴾. He praised the believers for their fear, saying: ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 50]. The mystics (arbab al-isharat) have expressions concerning fear that return to what we have mentioned. Al-Ustadh Abu ʿAli al-Daqqaq said: I entered upon Abu Bakr ibn Furak, may Allah have mercy on him, visiting him when he was ill. When he saw me, his eyes filled with tears. I said to him: "May Allah grant you health and cure." He said to me: "Do you think I fear death? I only fear what comes after death."

In Sunan Ibn Majah, from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I see what you do not see, and I hear what you do not hear. The sky creaks (ataṭṭat), and it has every right to creak, for there is no place of four fingers in it without an angel placing his forehead in prostration to Allah. By Allah, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, you would not enjoy women on your beds, and you would go out to the roads (al-saʿadat) crying out (tajarun) to Allah. By Allah, I wish I were a tree that is cut down." [[al-Ataṭṭ: the sound of camel saddles; ataṭ al-ibil: their sounds and moaning. That is, the great number of angels in the heavens has weighed upon it until it creaks. This is a figure of speech indicating the multitude of angels, even if there is no actual creaking; it is a way of bringing near, intended to establish the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (from Ibn al-Athir).]] [[Tajarun: they raise their voices in supplication, humbly.]] [[Taʿadud: cut with a ma'did (a tool for cutting trees).]] Al-Tirmidhi recorded it and said: "A hasan gharib hadith." It is also narrated by another route that Abu Dharr said: "I wish I were a tree that is cut." And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 3, verse 176:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you﴾. These were people who embraced Islam and then apostatized out of fear of the polytheists, so the Prophet (ﷺ) was saddened, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed: "Let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you." Al-Kalbi said: It refers to the hypocrites and the leaders of the Jews, who concealed the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Book, so this was revealed. It is also said: When the People of the Book did not believe, this grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because people looked at them and said, "They are People of the Book; if his words were true, they would have followed him." So the verse "Let not [it] grieve you" was revealed.

The recitation (qira'ah) of Nafi' is with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy wherever it occurs, except in al-Anbiya' (in "the greatest terror will not grieve them" [21:103]), where it is with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the zāy. Abu Ja'far recited the opposite of this. Ibn Muhaysin recited all of them with a damma on the yā' and [a kasra] on the zāy. [[All the original manuscripts read: a damma on the yā' and the zāy. The correct reading is what we have recorded. See p. 346, vol. 11.]] The rest recited all of them with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the zāy.

Both are dialectal forms: "ḥazananī al-amr yaḥzununī" and "aḥzananī" also, though the latter [dialect] is rare, and the first is the more eloquent of the two forms, as stated by al-Nahhas. A poet said, using "aḥzana":

"My companions passed away, and the dwellings saddened me."

The common recitation is "yusāri'ūna" (hasten). Talha recited "yusri'ūna fī al-kufr" (hasten in disbelief). Al-Dahhak said: They are the disbelievers of Quraysh. Others said: They are the hypocrites. It is also said: It is what we mentioned before. And it is said: It is general, applying to all disbelievers. Their hastening in disbelief is their active opposition to Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Qushayri said: Grief over the disbelief of a disbeliever is an act of obedience, but the Prophet (ﷺ) used to go to excess in grieving over the disbelief of his people, so he was forbidden from that, as He said: ﴿So let not your soul expire in regret over them﴾ [35:8] [[See vol. 14, p. 324.]], and He said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their following it, if they do not believe in this message, in sorrow﴾ [18:6] [[See vol. 10, p. 353.]]. ﴿Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾ — that is, they will not diminish anything of Allah's dominion and authority; meaning, their disbelief does not diminish it. This is like what is narrated from Abu Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning what he related from Allah, blessed and exalted is He, that He said: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another. O My servants, all of you are astray except those whom I have guided, so seek guidance from Me and I will guide you. O My servants, all of you are hungry except those whom I have fed, so seek food from Me and I will feed you. O My servants, all of you are naked except those whom I have clothed, so seek clothing from Me and I will clothe you. O My servants, you sin by night and by day, and I forgive all sins, so seek forgiveness from Me and I will forgive you. O My servants, you will never reach My harm so as to harm Me, and you will never reach My benefit so as to benefit Me. O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were upon the most pious heart of one man among you, that would not increase anything in My dominion. O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were upon the most wicked heart of one man, that would not decrease anything of My dominion. O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, stood in one open plain and asked Me, and I gave each person what he asked, that would not diminish what I have except as a needle diminishes when it is put into the sea. O My servants, it is only your deeds that I count for you, and then I repay you for them. So whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame no one but himself." Muslim recorded it in his Sahih, as did al-Tirmidhi and others. It is a great hadith, lengthy, which would be written out in full.

It is also said: The meaning of "they will never harm Allah at all" is: they will never harm the friends of Allah when they abandon their support, since Allah the Mighty and Majestic is their helper.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah intends not to give them a share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment﴾. That is, a portion. The ḥaẓẓ (share) means portion and good fortune. It is said: So-and-so is more fortunate (aḥẓẓ) than so-and-so, and he is blessed with fortune (maḥẓūẓ). The plural of ḥaẓẓ is aḥāẓ, against the usual pattern [[al-Jawhari said: It seems to be the plural of aḥẓ. Ibn Barri said: His statement "aḥāẓ against the usual pattern" is an error on his part; rather, aḥāẓ is the plural of aḥẓ, whose origin is aḥẓẓ, then the second ẓā' was changed to yā', becoming aḥẓ, and then it was pluralized as aḥāẓ.

(From al-Lisan.)]]. Abu Zayd said: One says "rajul ḥaẓīẓ," meaning fortunate, if he has a share of provision. And "ḥaẓiẓtu fī al-amr aḥaẓẓu" [I was fortunate in the matter]. The word ḥaẓẓ is sometimes pluralized as aḥuẓẓan, meaning: He does not make for them a share in Paradise. This is explicit evidence that good and evil occur by the will of Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 3, verse 177:

Allah's statement: ﴿Indeed, those who have exchanged disbelief for faith﴾ has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 210.]].

(They will never harm Allah in the least) is repeated for emphasis. It has also been said: meaning, because of the poor judgment of exchanging faith for disbelief and selling it for it, they do not fear His side or His planning. The word "shay'an" (in the least) is in the accusative in both places because it occupies the position of the verbal noun (masdar), as if he had said: they will never harm Allah with a small harm or a great harm. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by assuming the omission of the preposition "ba'" (with), as if he had said: they will never harm Allah with anything.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 3, verse 178:

Allah's words: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our granting them respite is good for their souls﴾. Al-imla' (respite) is the lengthening of life and the abundance of ease in living. The meaning is: let not those who frighten the Muslims suppose that Allah is unable to destroy them. Their lives are only prolonged so that they may commit sins, not because it is good for them. It is also said that the words "Our granting them respite" refer to the victory they achieved at the Battle of Uhud: that was not good for their souls, but it was so that they might increase in punishment. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "There is no one, whether righteous or wicked, but death is better for him. As for the righteous, Allah says: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 198] [[See p. 322 of this part.]]. As for the wicked, Allah says: (Verily, We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin)."

Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "lā yaḥsabanna" with the letter yā' and a fatha on the sīn. Hamza read it with the letter tā' and a fatha on the sīn. The rest read it with yā' and a kasra on the sīn. Whoever reads with yā', the subject (al-fa'il) is "alladhina" (those who), meaning: "let not the disbelievers suppose." The clause "Our granting them respite is good for their souls" fills the place of the two objects. "Anna-ma" here means "alladhi" (that which), the returning pronoun is omitted, and "khayr" is the predicate of "anna." It is also permissible to take "ma" together with the verb as a verbal noun, so the estimate becomes: "let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our granting them respite is good for their souls."

Whoever reads with tā', the subject is the addressee, who is Muhammad (ﷺ). "Alladhina" is in the accusative as the first object of "taḥsab." "Anna" and what follows it are in apposition (badal) to "alladhina," and they fill the place of both objects, just as they would do if they were not in apposition. It is not valid for "anna" and what follows it to be the second object of "taḥsab," because in this construction the second object is the first in meaning, since "ḥasiba" and its sisters govern the subject and predicate. So the estimate would be: "And do not suppose that Our granting them respite is good." This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Abu 'Ali said: "If this were correct, he would have said 'khayran' in the accusative, because 'anna' would become an apposition to 'alladhina kafaru,' as if he had said: 'Do not suppose that the granting of respite to those who disbelieve is good.' So his words 'khayran' would be the second object of 'ḥasiba.' Therefore it is not permissible to read 'lā taḥsabanna' with the tā' unless 'inna' in 'innama' is pronounced with a kasra and 'khayran' is in the accusative. This is not related from Hamza, and the reading from Hamza is with the tā', so this reading is not valid."

Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: "The reading of Hamza is permissible by way of repetition (al-takrir). Its estimate is: 'And let not those who disbelieve suppose,' and 'let not you suppose that Our granting them respite is good.' So 'anna' fills the place of the two objects: the second object of 'taḥsab,' and 'anna' with what it governs is the second object of 'taḥsab' in its first position."

Al-Qushayri said: "This is close to what al-Zajjaj mentioned concerning the claim of apposition, and the reading is sound." So Abu 'Ali's aim was to refute al-Zajjaj.

Al-Nahhas said: "Abu Hatim claimed that Hamza's reading with the tā' here, and His words: ﴿And let not those who withhold﴾ [Al 'Imran: 180], are a grammatical error (lahn) which is not permissible." A group followed him in this.

I say: This is not correct, because of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) already explained, and because the reading is sound and established by transmission. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "innama numli lahum" with the kasra on "inna" in both places. Abu Ja'far said: "The reading of Yahya is good, just as you say: 'I supposed 'Amr, his father is Khalid.'" Abu Hatim said: "I heard al-Akhfash mention the kasra of 'inna,' citing it as evidence for the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), because he was one of them. He would make the arrangement by transposition: 'And let not those who disbelieve suppose. Verily, We grant them respite that they may increase in sin. Verily, We grant them respite; it is good for their souls.'" He said: "I saw in a copy of the Qur'an in the Friday mosque that they had added a letter, so that it read 'innama numli lahum imanan' (We grant them respite that they may increase in faith). Ya'qub the reader looked at it, recognised the error, and scraped it out."

The verse is a clear text refuting the doctrine of the Qadariyya, because it informs us that Allah lengthens their lives so that they may increase in disbelief through committing sins, and the continual succession of their like upon the heart, as has already been explained concerning its opposite, which is faith.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "There is no one, whether righteous or wicked, but death is better for him." Then he recited: ﴿Verily, We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾, and he recited: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾. Related by Razin.

Abu al-Aliyah said: The believers asked to be given a sign by which they could distinguish the believer from the hypocrite, so Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the bad from the good﴾ — the verse. The commentators differed over who is addressed in the verse, giving several opinions. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and most of the mufassirun (commentators) said: the address is to the disbelievers and the hypocrites, meaning: Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in of disbelief, hypocrisy and enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi said: The Quraysh of Makkah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man from among us, you claim, is in the Fire; and if he leaves our religion and follows yours, you say he is among the people of Paradise! So tell us, from where is this? Tell us who among us comes to you, and who does not come to you?" So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: "Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in" of disbelief and hypocrisy, "until He distinguishes the bad from the good."

It was also said: the address is to the polytheists. By "the believers" in His words "to leave the believers" is meant those in the loins and wombs who will believe; that is, Allah would not leave your children, whom He has judged to be believers, in the state you are in of polytheism, until He separates them from you. On this view, ﴿Nor would Allah reveal to you the unseen﴾ is a new (independent) statement. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and most of the mufassirun.

It was also said: the address is to the believers, meaning: Allah would not leave you, O company of believers, in the state you are in of the mixing of the believer with the hypocrite, until He distinguishes between you by trial and obligation, so that you know the wicked hypocrite and the good believer. The Day of Uhud did distinguish between the two groups. This is the view of most of the people of meanings (scholars of the meanings of the Qur'an).

﴿Nor would Allah reveal to you the unseen﴾ — O company of believers, meaning: Allah would not single out the hypocrites for you so that you could recognise them; rather, this becomes apparent to you through obligation and trial. This did become apparent on the Day of Uhud, when the hypocrites held back and showed their gloating. You did not know this unseen matter before this, but now Allah has informed Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his companions of it. It was also said: the meaning of "to reveal to you" is: nor would Allah inform you of what will come from them. On this view, His words "Nor would Allah reveal to you [the unseen]" are connected (to what precedes); on the two earlier views they are disconnected. That is because when the disbelievers said, "Why has revelation not come to us?", He said: "Nor would Allah reveal to you the unseen" — that is, regarding who deserves prophethood, so that revelation would come according to your choice.

﴿But Allah chooses﴾ — that is, selects — ﴿from His messengers﴾ for the disclosure of His unseen — ﴿whom He wills﴾. It is said: "ṭalaʿtu ʿalā kadhā" and "iṭṭalaʿtu ʿalayhi," and "aṭlaʿtu ʿalayhi ghayrī," so it is both intransitive and transitive. It is also read "ḥattā yamīza" with the shaddah, from "mayyaza" (ḥamzah's reading), and likewise in "al-Anfal" (see vol. 7, p. 400). The rest read "yamīza" without the shaddah, from "māza yamīzu." It is said: "miztu al-shayʾa baʿḍahu min baʿḍin, amīzuhu mayzan, wa-mayyaztuhu tamyīzan." Abu Muʿadh said: "miztu al-shayʾa amīzuhu mayzan" when you separate two things; if they are many things, you say "mayyaztuhā tamyīzan." And similarly, when you make one thing into two, you say "farraqtu baynahumā" (lightened), and from it "farraqa al-shaʿr" (he parted the hair). If you make it into many things, you say "farraqtuhu tafrīqan." I say: from it also comes "imtāza al-qawm" (the people became distinct), "tamayyaza baʿḍuhum ʿan baʿḍin" (some of them became separated from others). And "yakādu yatamayyaz" means "it is cut apart," and it is with this meaning that His words, exalted is He, are explained: ﴿It almost bursts apart with rage﴾ [al-Mulk: 8] (see vol. 18, p. 218). In a report: "Whoever removes harm from the road, it is for him a charity."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾. It is said: when the disbelievers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to make clear to them which of them would believe, Allah revealed: "So believe in Allah and His messengers" — meaning: do not occupy yourselves with what does not concern you, and occupy yourselves with what does concern you, which is faith.

﴿So believe﴾ — that is, affirm; that is, your duty is affirmation, not eagerness to gain knowledge of the unseen.

﴿And if you believe and fear God, you will have a great reward﴾ — that is, Paradise. It is related that a man who was an astrologer was with al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi. Al-Hajjaj took pebbles in his hand whose number he knew, and said to the astrologer: "How many are in my hand?" The astrologer calculated and was correct. Then al-Hajjaj distracted him, and took pebbles which he did not count, and said to the astrologer: "How many are in my hand?" He calculated and was wrong; then he calculated again and was wrong. He said: "Honourable Amir, I think you do not know the number of what is in your hand?" He said: "No." He said: "What is the difference between the two?" He said: "That one you had counted, so it went out of the realm of the unseen, and I calculated and was correct; but this one you did not know the number of, so it became unseen, and none knows the unseen but Allah, exalted is He." This topic will come again in "al-An'am" (see vol. 7, p. 1 onward), God willing.

There are four issues here.

**First issue:** The word *alladhina* (﴿الَّذِينَ﴾) is in the nominative position (*fi mawdi' raf'*), and the first object of the verb is omitted. Al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Farra' said: the meaning is "the miserliness is better for them," that is, "let not those who are miserly suppose that miserliness is better for them." It was omitted because *yabkhaluna* ("they are miserly") indicates *al-bukhl* ("miserliness"). This is like the saying: "whoever is truthful, it is good for him," meaning "truthfulness is good for him." From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When the foolish man is forbidden, he rushes toward it, and opposes, and the foolish man turns to opposition."*

So the meaning is: he rushes toward foolishness; the *safih* (foolish man) indicates *safah* (foolishness). As for the reading of Hamzah with the *ta'* (﴿تَحْسَبَنَّ﴾), it is very weak, as al-Nahhas said. Its permissibility lies in the estimate: "Do not suppose that the miserliness of those who are miserly is better for them." Al-Zajjaj said: it is like "and ask the town" (Yusuf 12:82). The word "huwa" in "huwa khayran lahum" is a separator (*fasila*) according to the Basrans, and a pillar (*'imad*) according to the Kufans. Al-Nahhas said: it is also permissible in Arabic to say "huwa khayrun lahum" as a subject and predicate.

**Second issue:** ﴿بَلْ هُوَ شَرٌّ لَهُمْ﴾ is a subject and predicate: that is, "miserliness is evil for them." The *sin* in "sayutawwaqun" is *sin al-wa'id* (the sin of threat), meaning "they will be girded," as al-Mubarrad said.

This verse was revealed about withholding wealth from spending in the way of God and paying the obligatory zakat. It is like His saying: ﴿and they do not spend it in the way of God﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:34), and so on. A group of the commentators held this view, among them Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Wa'il, Abu Malik, al-Suddi and al-Sha'bi. They said: the meaning of "sayutawwaqun ma bakhilu bih" is what is recorded in the hadith from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever God gives wealth but does not pay its zakat, on the Day of Resurrection his wealth will be made into a bald, venomous serpent [*shuja'*: the male viper, or the one that rises on its tail and leaps at the walker or rider] with two black spots above its eyes [*zabibatan*], which will coil around him on the Day of Resurrection, then seize him by his two jaws [*lahzimatayh*], and then say: 'I am your wealth, I am your treasure.'" Then he recited this verse: ﴿And let not those who are miserly suppose...﴾ [the verse]. This was related by al-Nasa'i. [This is the narration of al-Bukhari from Abu Hurayrah, and its wording. As for what al-Nasa'i related, it is a different wording from Ibn Mas'ud. See Sahih al-Bukhari and Sunan al-Nasa'i, in the chapter on zakat.] Ibn Majah also related it from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "No one who does not pay the zakat of his wealth will fail to have it made into a bald serpent on the Day of Resurrection, which will be placed around his neck." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to us its confirmation from the Book of God, the Exalted: ﴿And let not those who are miserly with what God has given them of His bounty suppose...﴾ [the verse].

There also came from him (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no close relative who comes to his close relative asking him for some of what he has, and he is miserly with him, but on the Day of Resurrection a serpent from Hell will be brought out for him, flicking its tongue [*yatalammazu*: it extends its tongue like one licking food], until it coils around him."

Ibn 'Abbas also said: it was revealed only about the People of the Book and their miserliness in clarifying what they knew about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). Mujahid and a group of the scholars said the same. On this interpretation, the meaning of "sayutawwaqun" is that they will bear the punishment for what they were miserly with. So it derives from *al-taqah* (capacity), as He said: ﴿and for those who are able to do it﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:184), and it is not from *al-tatwiq* (girding).

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: the meaning of "sayutawwaqun" is that on the Day of Resurrection a collar of fire will be made for them. This accords with the first interpretation, and that is the view of al-Suddi. It is also said: they will be bound to their deeds, as a collar binds the neck. It is said: "so-and-so was girded with his deed like the collar of a dove," meaning his deed was bound to him. God the Exalted said: ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck﴾ (al-Isra' 17:13). [See vol. 10, p. 229.]

From this meaning is the verse of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh to Abu Sufyan:

*"Convey to Abu Sufyan, concerning a matter whose consequences are regret:*
*the house of your cousin you sold, to pay off your debt by it.*
*And your ally by God, Lord of the people, is striving in the oath.*
*Take it, take it! You have been girded with it, the girding of the dove."*

[When the Banu Jahsh emigrated from Mecca to Medina, they left their houses locked, with no one living in them. Abu Sufyan sold them to 'Amr ibn 'Alqamah. 'Abd Allah said these verses to Abu Sufyan after the conquest of Mecca. See Ibn Hisham's Sirah, p. 339, Europe edition.]

This accords with the second interpretation.

Miserliness (*al-bukhl*) in the language means that a person withholds the right that is obligatory on him. As for one who withholds what is not obligatory on him, he is not miserly, because he is not blamed for that. The people of the Hijaz say "yabkhulun" and "qad bakhalu," while the rest of the Arabs say "bakhilu yabkhalun." This is related by al-Nahhas. And "bakhila yabkhalu bukhlan wa bakhalan" is from Ibn Faris.

**Third issue:** On the fruit and benefit of miserliness: it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar: "Who is your chief?" They said: "Al-Jadd ibn Qays, though he has a miserliness in him." He (ﷺ) said: "And what disease is more harmful than miserliness?" [*ayy da' adwa*: what defect is uglier than it]. They said: "How is that, O Messenger of God?" He said: "A people settled on the seashore, and because of their miserliness they disliked the visit of guests to them. So they said: 'Let the men keep away from us from the women, until the men make excuses to the guests by the distance of the women, and the women make excuses by the distance of the men.' They did so, and this continued for them, so the men became occupied with men and the women with women." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi in *Adab al-Dunya wa al-Din*. And God knows best.

**Fourth issue:** There is disagreement about *al-bukhl* and *al-shuhh* (avarice): are they one meaning or two? It is said: *al-bukhl* is refraining from giving out what you already possess, and *al-shuhh* is greed for acquiring what you do not possess. It is also said: *al-shuhh* is miserliness together with greed, and this is the sound view, because of what Muslim related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Beware of injustice, for injustice will be darknesses on the Day of Resurrection. And beware of *shuhh*, for *shuhh* destroyed those before you: it drove them to shed their blood and make lawful what was forbidden to them."

This refutes the view of those who say that *bukhl* is withholding what is obligatory and *shuhh* is withholding what is recommended, because if *shuhh* were withholding what is recommended, it would not fall under this great threat and severe censure, which bring about the ruin of this world and the next [in one copy: "the ruin of this world, the next, and the religion"].

This meaning is supported by what al-Nasa'i related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Dust in the way of God and the smoke of Hell never gather in the nostrils of a Muslim man, and *shuhh* and faith never gather in the heart of a Muslim man." This shows that *shuhh* is more severely blamed than *bukhl*. However, there is also what shows that they are equal: he was asked, "Can a believer be miserly?" He said: "No."

Al-Mawardi mentioned in *Adab al-Dunya wa al-Din* that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar: "Who is your chief?" They said: "Al-Jadd ibn Qays, though he has a miserliness in him," [and] the hadith [continues]. It has already been mentioned.

**The words of God, the Exalted:** ﴿And to God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾. He, the Exalted, informs us of His permanence and the everlastingness of His dominion, and that He is, in eternity as He is in pre-eternity, independent of the worlds. He inherits the earth after the annihilation of His creation and the passing of their possessions, so the possessions and wealth remain with no claimant. This has taken the course of inheritance in the customary usage of people, but it is not inheritance in reality, because the true heir is one who inherits something he did not previously own. God, glorified and exalted, is the owner of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. The heavens and what is in them, and the earth and what is in it, belonged to Him all along. The wealth was a loan with its owners, and when they die, the loan is returned to its owner, to whom it belonged originally. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it﴾ (Maryam 19:40) [see vol. 11, p. 105], and so on. The meaning of both verses is that God, the Exalted, commanded His servants to spend and not to be miserly before they die and leave that as an inheritance to God, the Exalted, and nothing will benefit them except what they spent.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 3, verses 181–182:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah has heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor, and we are rich."﴾ He, exalted is He, mentioned the ugliness of the statement of the disbelievers, especially the Jews. The people of tafsir said: When Allah revealed ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245] [[See vol. 2, p. 237.]], a group of the Jews – among them Huyayy ibn Akhtab, according to al-Hasan's view – said. And ʿIkrimah and others said: it was Finhas ibn ʿAzura, who said: "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich; He borrows from us." They only said this to deceive their weak-minded followers, not because they actually believed it, for they were People of the Book. Yet they disbelieved by this statement, because they intended to create doubt among the weak amongst them and among the believers, and to deny the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: He is poor according to the saying of Muhammad ﷺ, since he borrowed from us.

(We will record what they said and will recompense them for it. It was also said: We will write it in their records of deeds, meaning We command the recording angels to register their statement, so that they will read it on the Day of Resurrection in the books they are given, so that it becomes more emphatic as proof against them. This is like His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are its recorders﴾ [al-Anbiya': 94] [[See vol. 12, p. 339.]]. It was also said: the purpose of writing is preservation, meaning: We will preserve what they said in order to recompense them. The "mā" in His saying "mā qālū" is in the accusative position governed by "sanaktub." Al-Aʿmash and Hamzah read "sayaktubu" with the ya', so "mā" is the subject of the passive verb. Hamzah based this on the reading of Ibn Masʿud: "wa-yuqālu dhūqū ʿadhāba al-ḥarīq.")

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their killing of the prophets without right﴾, meaning: and We will record their killing of the prophets, that is, their approval of killing. The intended reference is the killing of their ancestors of the prophets, but since they approved of it, the attribution to them was valid. A man praised the killing of ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, in the presence of al-Shaʿbi, and al-Shaʿbi said to him: "You shared in his blood." Thus he made approval of killing to be killing, may Allah be pleased with him.

I say: This is a great issue, where approval of disobedience is itself disobedience. Abu Dawud related from al-ʿUrs ibn ʿUmayrah al-Kindi, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "When a sin is committed on earth, whoever witnesses it and dislikes it – and he said once: and denounces it – is like one who was absent from it, and whoever is absent from it and approves of it is like one who witnessed it." And this is a clear text.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without right﴾, its meaning has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 431.]]. (And We will say: "Taste the punishment of the burning.") That is, it will be said to them in Hell, or at death, or at the reckoning: this. Then, whether this statement is from Allah, exalted is He, or from the angels, is two opinions. The reading of Ibn Masʿud is "wa-yuqal." Al-Ḥarīq is the name for flaming fire, while "al-nār" includes both flaming and non-flaming fire.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is for what your hands have put forth﴾, meaning: that punishment is for the sins previously committed. The hands are specifically mentioned to indicate direct undertaking and performance of the act, since an act may be attributed to a person in the sense that he ordered it, as in His saying: ﴿slaughtering their sons﴾ [al-Qasas: 4] [[See vol. 13, p. 247.]]. The original form of "aydīkum" is "aydiykum," and the damma was dropped because of its heaviness. And Allah knows best.

And this is a clear text.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without right﴾, its meaning has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 431.]]. (And We will say: "Taste the punishment of the burning.") That is, it will be said to them in Hell, or at death, or at the reckoning: this. Then, whether this statement is from Allah, exalted is He, or from the angels, is two opinions. The reading of Ibn Masʿud is "wa-yuqal." Al-Ḥarīq is the name for flaming fire, while "al-nār" includes both flaming and non-flaming fire.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is for what your hands have put forth﴾, meaning: that punishment is for the sins previously committed. The hands are specifically mentioned to indicate direct undertaking and performance of the act, since an act may be attributed to a person in the sense that he ordered it, as in His saying: ﴿slaughtering their sons﴾ [al-Qasas: 4] [[See vol. 13, p. 247.]]. The original form of "aydīkum" is "aydiykum," and the damma was dropped because of its heaviness. And Allah knows best.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah Al ʿImran, verses 183–184:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who﴾ (*alladhina*) are in the genitive case as a substitute (*badal*) for "those who" in His words, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said﴾. Or they are a qualifier (*naʿt*) for "the servants" (*lil-ʿabid*), or the predicate of an inceptive (*khabar mubtadaʾ*), meaning: they are those who said. Al-Kalbi and others said: it was revealed concerning Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Wahb ibn Yahudha, Finhas ibn ʿAzura, and a group who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: "Do you claim that Allah sent you to us, and that He revealed to us a book in which He charged us not to believe in any messenger who claims that he is from Allah until he brings us a sacrifice (*qurban*) that fire consumes? If you bring it to us, we will believe you." So Allah revealed this verse. It was said: this was in the Torah, but the complete statement was: "until there comes to you the Messiah and Muhammad; when they come to you, believe in them both without a sacrifice."

It was also said: the matter of sacrifices remained in force until it was abrogated (*nusikha*) by the tongue of ʿIsa ibn Maryam. The prophet among them would slaughter and supplicate, and a white fire with a crackling sound and no smoke would descend and consume the sacrifice. So this claim was a pretension of the Jews, since there was an exception (*istithnaʾ*) in it, which they concealed, or it was abrogated; and in their clinging to it they were being obstinate. The miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ) are a decisive proof in refuting their claim, and likewise the miracles of ʿIsa. Whoever's truthfulness is obligatory, his truthfulness must be affirmed.

Then He, exalted is He, said, establishing the proof against them: ﴿Say﴾ (O Muhammad), ﴿"Messengers before me have certainly come to you﴾ (O people of the Book), ﴿with clear proofs and with what you mention﴾ (of the sacrifice), ﴿so why did you kill them, if you are truthful?"﴾ meaning Zakariyya, Yahya, Shaʿya, and all the other prophets, peace be upon them, whom they killed and whom they did not believe. By this He meant their predecessors. This verse is the one that ʿAmir al-Shaʿbi, may Allah be pleased with him, recited, and he used it as evidence against the one who justified the killing of ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, as we have explained. Allah, exalted is He, called the Jews killers because of their approval of the deeds of their predecessors, even though there was between them about seven hundred years.

The *qurban* is what one draws near to Allah, exalted is He, by, of acts of worship (*nusuk*), charity, and righteous deeds. It is on the pattern *fuʿlān* from *al-qurba* (nearness). It can be a noun and a verbal noun (*masdar*). The pattern of the noun is *al-sultan* and *al-burhan*, and the verbal noun is *al-ʿudwan* and *al-khusran*. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar used to read *bi-qurbanin* with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* (*bi-qurbunin*), following the *ḍamma* of the *qāf*, just as it is said in the plural of *ẓulmah* (darkness): *ẓulumat*, and in *ḥujrah* (chamber): *ḥujurat*.

Then He, exalted is He, said, consoling His Prophet and comforting him: ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs﴾, meaning with indications (*dalalat*).

﴿And the scriptures﴾, meaning the written books (*al-kutub al-mazbura*), i.e., the written ones. *Zubur* is the plural of *zabur*, which means book, and its origin is from *zabartu*, meaning I wrote. Every *zabur* is a book. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"For a campsite I saw, which stirred my longing, like the writing of a script on a Yemeni palm-frond stalk (ʿasīb)."*

*(Note: the ʿasīb is the palm frond from which a leaflet has been stripped, that is, the stalk.)*

"And I know its *tazbirah*," i.e., its writing. It was also said: *zabur* derives from *zabr*, meaning rebuke. One says *zabartu al-rajul*, meaning I rebuked the man; and *zabartu al-bi'r*, meaning I lined the well with stones.

Ibn ʿAmir read *"bil-zuburi wa bil-kitabi al-munir"* with an added *bāʾ* in both words. And so it is in the codices of the people of Syria.

﴿And the illuminating book﴾, i.e., the clear, evident one, from your saying *anartu al-shayʾa uniruhu*, meaning I made the thing clear. It is said: *nāra al-shayʾ*, *anarahu*, *nawwarahu*, and *istanarahu* with the same meaning, and each of these is both intransitive and transitive. He combined *al-zubur* and *al-kitab*, although they have the same meaning, because their wordings differ, and their origin is as we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 3, verse 185 (part 1 of 2):

There are seven [[As in the manuscripts; the division gives eight, but seven is what is relied upon.]] issues in it.

**The first issue:** When Allah, may He be exalted, reported about the miserly and their disbelief in their saying, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich," and commanded the believers to be patient over their harm in His saying, ﴿You will surely be tested﴾ [Al 'Imran: 186], and so on, He made clear that this is something that passes and does not last, for the lifespan of this world is short, and the Day of Resurrection is the Day of Recompense.

﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ is from "dhawq" (tasting). This is something from which no human can escape, and from which no living creature can flee. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*Whoever does not die in his prime [[Mata 'abtatan: i.e., young and healthy.]] will die of old age;*
*death is a cup, and a man is its taster.*

Another said:

*Death is a gate, and all people enter it;*
*so I wonder what the house is, after the gate.*

**The second issue:** The common reading is "dha'iqatu al-mawt" with the construct (idafa). Al-A'mash, Yahya and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "dha'iqatun al-mawta" with tanwin and the accusative on "al-mawt." They said: because it has not yet tasted. The active participle (ism al-fa'il) has two forms: one denotes past time, and the other denotes future time. If you intend the first, there is only the idafa to what follows it, as in your saying, "This is the one who struck Zayd yesterday" and "the slayer of Bakr yesterday," because it functions like a fixed noun, namely a proper noun, such as "the boy of Zayd" and "the companion of Bakr." A poet said:

*The guardians of the honour of the clan, who are not*
*approached from behind by any defect [[al-wakf: a defect. The line belongs to 'Amr ibn Imru' al-Qays, and is also attributed to Qays ibn al-Khatim.*
*(from Lisan al-'Arab).]]*

If you intend the second, the genitive is permitted. The accusative and tanwin in a case of this kind is the original form, because it functions like the imperfect verb. If the verb is intransitive, it does not take an object, as in "Zayd is standing up" (qa'im). If it is transitive, you make it take an object and govern it in the accusative, so you say, "Zayd is one who strikes 'Amr" meaning "strikes 'Amr."

It is permissible to drop the tanwin and the idafa for lightness, as the poet al-Marrar said:

*Drive away the worries with every docile-headed one [[Qawluhu mu'ti ra'sahu: i.e., obedient. Naj: swift. Sahba: when its whiteness inclines towards red. Al-mut'ayyis and al-u'ays: white, which is the finest colour of camels. The meaning: drive away your persistent worries caused by the separation from the one you love and distance from him, with every camel you ride for travel.]]*
*swift, mixed with reddish-white, white-coloured,*
*[[He described a camel with a large belly; when he fastens its saddle upon it, he takes its ropes (plural of habl) and fills them out because of its large belly. Al-ightiyal: to carry something away. Al-mubin: the long one. Zabana: he jostled and pushed. Al-'arandas: the strong one. It is also narrated as: "strong of neck" (matin 'unuquhu).*
*(from Sharh al-Shawahid by al-Shantamari).]]*
*who takes its ropes, its neck strong, among the shoulder that pushes the camels, mighty.*

Here he dropped the tanwin for lightness, and the original is "mu'tin ra'sahu" with tanwin and the accusative. Similar to this in the Revelation is His saying, ﴿Are they removers of His harm?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 38], and what is similar to it [[The addition is from j, t, d and h.]].

**The third issue:** Know that death has causes and signs. Among the signs of a believer's death is the sweat of the forehead. An-Nasa'i reported it from the hadith of Buraydah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, "The believer dies with the sweat of the forehead." We have explained this in *at-Tadhkirah*. When someone is dying, they should be prompted to say the testimony of faith, due to the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Prompt your dying ones to say, 'There is no god but Allah,'" so that it will be his last words, and he will end with the testimony of faith. It should not be repeated to him, lest he become annoyed. It is recommended to recite Surah Ya-Sin at that time, due to the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Recite Ya-Sin over your dying ones," reported by Abu Dawud. Al-Ajurri mentioned in *Kitab an-Nasihah*, from the hadith of Umm ad-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No dying person over whom Surah Ya-Sin is recited, except that death is made easy for him."

When the soul is taken and the gaze follows the spirit, as the Prophet (ﷺ) informed in Sahih Muslim, and acts of worship are lifted and legal obligation ceases, rulings become binding on the living. Among them: closing his eyes. And informing his righteous brothers of his death. Some people disliked it and said: it is from *na'y* (announcing a death in a way that is forbidden). The first view is more sound, and we have explained this in another place. Among them: hastening to prepare him by washing and burial, lest decay quickly set in. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to a people who delayed the burial of their dead: "Hasten the burial of your corpse," and he said, "Hasten the funeral," the hadith continues, and it will come.

**The fourth issue:** As for washing him, it is a *sunnah* for all Muslims, except the martyr, as already mentioned. It has been said that washing him is obligatory. This was said by al-Qadi 'Abd al-Wahhab. The first view is the position of the book [[So in all the manuscripts.]], and scholars hold both of these opinions.
